To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we present the first rates for flares in the NIR, and we show that flares in the optical and NIR have different properties.
we have measured the rates of flares on M dwarfs in eight photometric filters, and we have determined the detection thresholds for flaring M dwarfs in the optical and near-in infrared (NIR).
the frequency of optical flares is in agreement with previous results, but the frequency of NIR flares is two orders of magnitude below that of optical flares.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of stellar flares on low-mass stars, in particular M dwarf stars.
the characterization of the stellar flare phenomenon, which is a key component to understanding stellar variability and the impact of stellar activity on habitability.
the characterization of stellar flares on low-mass stars using SDSS and 2MASS time-domain surveys.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the flaring rates in the optical are consistent with previous results but that the rates in the infrared are much smaller.
the flaring rates in the optical bands are in good agreement with previous studies and the flare rates in the NIR bands are lower by two orders of magnitude.
M dwarfs do flare in the NIR and the rates are low.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we find that the NIR flaring rate for M0-M6 stars is ~1.5 flares per hour per star, while the optical flaring rate is ~0.2 per hour.
the flare detection rate in the NIR is much lower than in the optical and the NIR is more sensitive to flares of lower amplitude.
we have shown the first flare rates for M dwarfs in NIR filters.
The main takeaway from our work is that
flares are not only a problem for optical observations of M dwarfs but can also affect NIR observations.
the NIR is a valuable wavelength range for detecting flares on M dwarfs, and that flares are not limited to the optical.
the NIR will be the best wavelength for detecting the largest-amplitude flares from M dwarfs.
